title: Design exercise: LLM gateway
summary: Design a shared model gateway with tenant-scoped admission, streaming, provider-aware limits and privacy controls. Reserve worst-case request cost before dispatch, distinguish retry safety from billing certainty, and map hosted and self-hosted deployment choices to AWS.

exercise.prompt: Design the company's gateway to large language models: every internal application calls one API that fronts several hosted providers and a self-hosted model fleet. Teams get keys, quotas and budgets; the gateway retries and fails over safely, streams tokens, keeps spend visible, and logs enough to debug without leaking what users typed.

constraints.caption: Exercise assumptions and targets; not measured production values.
rows: One request format for chat completions and embeddings with streaming; per-team keys, token-based rate limits and monthly budgets; routing of a model alias to one or more deployments with fallback; retries that never duplicate a side effect; prompt caching where the provider supports it; request logging with redaction; spend attribution per team and per key.
200 teams; 5 million requests/day; peak 3 times average.
3,000 input tokens/request; 20 percent embeddings; chat averages 400 output tokens.
Two hosted providers and one self-hosted open-weight fleet.

Gateway overhead under 10 ms at p99 on top of the provider; first token streamed within 1 s at p50 for chat; 99.9 percent availability of the gateway itself (providers have their own); a team can never exceed its budget by more than one minute of traffic; no raw prompt is stored unless the team opted in.
Model quality evaluation itself, prompt authoring tools, fine-tuning, agent orchestration, the self-hosted model servers' internals (treated as deployments with a known capacity).

clarifying_questions.a: Both: the provider's limits per model class, expressed in requests per minute, input tokens per minute and output tokens per minute and signalled by a 429 with a retry-after header, and the gateway's own per-team limits, which must sum to less than the provider's.

Only an explicitly retryable outcome within the attempt budget. No first byte does not prove no inference or bill. Interrupted streams are not resumed or restarted transparently; same request id returns status, never a second dispatch.
Provider-supported prefixes, plus optional tenant-scoped exact responses under an explicit reuse policy. Temperature zero is not a determinism guarantee.

clarifying_questions.q: Can a request choose the provider?
clarifying_questions.a: It names a model alias; policy maps the alias to deployments in order. A team may pin a deployment for a test, never for production traffic.

Metadata always (team, key, model, route, tokens in and out, cached tokens, latency, status); prompt and completion text only for teams that opted in, after redaction of recognisable personal data, with a retention of 30 days (assumption).
Hard admission uses worst-case reservations for all allowed attempts, including in-flight unknown usage; the original one-minute target is strengthened. A 90 percent warning remains a policy setting.

blocks.text: The original latency argument assumed no network call on the hot path. Shared hard budgets need coordinated state, so that is not a proof of the overhead target. Measure admission, TLS and streaming under load; the proposed durable reservation path may require revisiting the target rather than calling an unmeasured number achieved.

A minute of delayed aggregation does not bound spend by itself: requests may be in flight much longer, and their final usage is unknown. This design strengthens the original contract with a worst-case reservation covering every allowed billable attempt before dispatch. The asynchronous usage log is for showback, not the authority that permits more spend.

Stateless gateway tasks enforce policy and proxy streams; durable request reservations coordinate spend. Local token buckets receive leased shares of a global provider limit rather than each assuming it owns the whole quota. Exact response caches are optional, tenant-scoped and bypassed when semantics or privacy prohibit reuse.

blocks.text: No vector-store fork applies to a gateway: embedding responses are passed through, not indexed here. A distributed response cache is deferred until measured repetition justifies it; temperature zero is not a determinism guarantee, and cached output is an explicit product reuse policy.

blocks.text: Reserve the upper cost of all allowed attempts before first dispatch, using the maximum accepted input, output cap and most expensive permitted route. Each attempt is charged or remains reserved when usage is unknown. A final atomic settlement moves known cost to spent, retains unknown exposure and releases only provably unused budget. Never release a crashed request’s reservation merely because its owner lease expired; reconciliation or conservative maximum charging resolves it.

The request record is both the idempotency claim and usage outbox. A transaction creates that record and increases the team’s reserved balance; a separate settlement transaction updates both records. Unknown requests cannot be resubmitted under the same id. This avoids pretending a provider call and a database transaction can commit atomically. A fresh id is a new billable request with its own reservation.

blocks.title: Admission, routing and settlement
items: Authenticate key and scope, enforce policy lease and count input locally. Lease global rate shares to nodes; expire old leases conservatively so a partition cannot multiply capacity.

Atomically claim the tenant/request key with payload hash and reserve the maximum of all permitted attempts. Insufficient budget fails closed; a duplicate reads existing status rather than dispatching again.
Choose a route allowed for this alias and data classification. Check per-provider request, input-token, output-token and concurrency dimensions; cache hits may affect these differently by provider.

A confirmed rejection before inference may permit bounded failover. An ambiguous timeout can have incurred usage even with no first byte; failover is allowed only under an explicit duplicate-inference policy with both attempt costs reserved. Never retry a tool side effect; tools are out of scope.

After any client-visible output, do not splice another completion into the same stream. Return an interrupted marker, not a fabricated resume cursor. The client may choose a new request with a new id and budget.
Settle known usage atomically against the reservation; retain unknown attempt exposure. Store the usage intent in the request record so a dispatcher can recover after a gateway crash.
Project usage asynchronously with event deduplication; the rollup’s delay never authorises additional spending. Show spent, reserved and unknown usage separately.

blocks.text: Provider quotas and in-flight model capacity are different limits. A global request rate alone cannot protect a model whose token lengths or stream durations grow. Lease bounded shares of each applicable quota class to gateway nodes and shed low-priority evaluations before customer-facing work. Bedrock embedding models are throttled by requests per minute, not tokens per minute, even though the selected Titan model is billed by input tokens. Stripe’s token-bucket implementation is a reference for the mechanism, not a universal model-provider quota contract.

blocks.caption: Pressure and control.
rows: Respect retry headers when present; bounded backoff and route health state.
Some spend-limit errors have no useful retry-after; classify error, do not retry forever.
Per-deployment in-flight limit and cancellation on client disconnect.
Cancellation is best effort; it does not guarantee no provider charge.
Measure contention; if necessary allocate durable prepaid sub-budgets without exceeding total.
A sharding plan must preserve the sum of outstanding grants, not duplicate the budget.
Existing short-lived leases only; fail closed after expiry.
Revocation window is explicit and acceptable to security.
Per-alias cache-hit ratio; preserve provider-required prefix identity.
A cacheable prefix is not a guaranteed cache hit.
Temperature zero does not establish determinism or freshness.

blocks.text: Metadata logs make routing and cost review possible; text retention is a separate permission. Redact before writing, separate access to opted-in text from aggregate usage, and retain enough request/attempt identifiers to reconcile unknown billing without storing prompts. The provider usage event and the client’s visible success are not the same fact.

blocks.caption: Failure modes.
rows: Classify rejection versus ambiguous processing; reserve every allowed attempt.
No transparent restart or invented resumability; new request is a new charge.
Fail closed; local rate buckets do not authorise spend.
Fail closed when lease expires; revocation lag is bounded, not indefinite.
Keep maximum reservation; do not transfer dispatch ownership and repeat the provider call.
Processed event and rollup delta in one transaction.
Early rejection or permitted hosted fallback
Per-model concurrency limiter and priority shedding.
Reconcile billing evidence; if unknowable, retain/charge the reserved maximum.

reference_answer.title: Trade-offs and the alternative not taken

blocks.caption: Central choices.
rows: Shared budgets, policies and spend need a common authority.
No single request metric describes model work.
No output does not mean no inference, charge or side effect.
In-flight and unknown usage invalidate the old minute-only bound.
Privacy and model-version semantics outweigh shared hit rate.
Debugging does not justify default prompt retention.

blocks.caption: Workload at scale, with the same averages.
rows: Explicit tenant tiers and isolated admission capacity.
Size streams by observed duration, not just requests.
Provider quota purchases and route placement matter.
Output caps and model quality gates remain central.
Upper bound; actual provider cache billing varies.

blocks.caption: Neutral model-cost sensitivity, assumed prices not provider quotes; no cache savings.

blocks.text: At company scale, review model alias changes as dependency upgrades: allowed data classes, quality, latency and billing all change together. Token showback can become chargeback only after unknown usage and attempt attribution are reconciled. Self-hosted capacity planning uses observed token lengths and concurrency per model; request counts alone cannot select a GPU fleet.

L1: One API in front of several providers with per-team keys, quotas, logging and retries, and the token arithmetic from the assumptions.
Streaming proxied end to end with the time to first token measured.
A retry rule that never duplicates output.
L2: Routing and fallback across hosted and self-hosted deployments with per-deployment breakers and observed limit state.
Token-based rate limits per team summing below the provider ceiling, with conservatively leased rate shares and durable spend reservations.
Prompt caching used deliberately (stable prefix first, breakpoint) with the pricing and limit consequences stated.
Budgets with worst-case attempt reservations, and personal data kept out of logs by default.
L3: A company-wide gateway: tenancy tiers, policy and guardrails in the path, evaluation of routing decisions from the log.
Cost allocation (showback to chargeback) and capacity planning for self-hosted models from observed demand.
What the gateway refuses: unbounded output, unredacted text by default, production traffic pinned to one deployment.

interview_frame.title: A 45-minute interview
items: 0:00 to 0:05: Requirements: whose limits matter, what a outcome-aware retry permits, what the cache caches, who chooses the provider, what is logged, hard or soft budgets. Say the numbers aloud: 174 requests per second at peak, 15 billion input tokens and 1.6 billion output tokens per day, 31 million input tokens per minute at peak against per-minute provider limits, about half of input tokens cacheable.

0:05 to 0:10: Entities and API: Team with limits and budget, Key, ModelAlias with ordered deployments, DeploymentState, RequestLog with cached tokens, Spend; the completions, embeddings and usage endpoints and the error classes.

0:10 to 0:20: High-level design with the diagram: gateway nodes, key and policy store, token counters, router to providers and the self-hosted fleet, response cache, redacted log, spend aggregator. Say which state is local and which is shared.

0:20 to 0:40: Two deep dives: limits and fairness under a shared provider ceiling (token buckets per team, concurrency per self-hosted deployment, shedding by priority, breakers and failover), then cost and privacy (prompt caching mechanics and prices, response cache, routing by policy, redaction and retention of logs, the in-flight reservation invariant).

0:40 to 0:45: Failure modes from the table, the 10x platform (tenancy tiers, guardrails, routing evaluation, chargeback, capacity planning), and the L3 sentence: the gateway is a rate limiter, a cost allocator and a privacy boundary that happens to proxy requests.
Context and scope: The applications calling models today, the providers and contracts, the self-hosted fleet's capacity, the spend surprise or the 429 incident that motivates the gateway.

Goals and non-goals: One API, team limits and budgets, safe failover, streaming, spend visibility, privacy by default; no evaluation product, no prompt tooling, no fine-tuning, no agent orchestration.
Design: This answer fills it: admission, routing, streaming proxy, settlement, the counter and log design, caching.
Alternatives considered: An SDK per app, request-based limits, retry-anything, synchronous exact budgets, always-on text logging, with the trade-off table.

Cross-cutting concerns: Security (key hashing, scopes, revocation propagation, admin audit), privacy (redaction, opt-in text, retention, access control on the log store), observability (first-token latency per deployment, failover ratio, cache hit ratio, spend per team per day, rejected requests by reason), cost (tokens by class per team), rollout by moving one team's alias at a time with the direct provider path as fallback.
Review questions the doc must answer: What a client receives when a stream breaks after the first token, and by how much a team can exceed its budget before the gate closes.
